## File: gl32prgd/lightbasics.html
```html
<!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD HTML 3.2//EN">
<HTML>

<!--gl32prgd/lightbasics.html Mon, 24 Jan 2022 16:28:07 GMT -->
<HEAD>
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=iso-8859-1">

   <TITLE>Lighting Basics
</TITLE>
   
</HEAD>

<body bgcolor="#fcfbf0">
<center>
[  <a href="lightintro.html">Previous</a>  |
<a href="advlightcap.html">Next</a>  |
<A HREF="toc.html" TARGET="_parent">Contents</A>  
 <A HREF="../gl32prgd/specialterms.html" TARGET="_parent">| Glossary</A>  
 <A HREF="topnav/topnav.html" TARGET="_top"></A>  
 <A HREF="cgi-bin/ds_form?config=/usr/share/man/info/en_US/a_doc_lib/data/base.cfg" TARGET="_top"></A>  ]
<hr>
<font color="#a62a2a" size="+2">
<i>GL3.2 Version 4.1 for AIX: Programming Concepts</i></font>
</center>
<hr size=3 noshade>



<H2><A NAME="lightbasics.html"></A>Lighting Basics </H2>


<P><A NAME="INDEX496"></A><A NAME="INDEX497"></A><A NAME="INDEX498"></A><A NAME="INDEX499"></A><A NAME="INDEX500"></A><A NAME="INDEX501"></A></P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80377mhay"></A>This section discusses the basic techniques
of lighting, including: </P>


<UL><LI><A NAME="A258C01bfbe"></A>A Simple <A HREF="lightbasics.html#A342C970d0">Lighting
Calculation</A></LI>


<LI><A NAME="A258C01bfbf"></A><A HREF="lightbasics.html#A342C970eb">Specularity</A></LI>


<LI><A NAME="A258C01bfc0"></A>Multiple Surface Materials and <A HREF="lightbasics.html#A342C97101">Multiple
Lights</A></LI></UL>


<H3><A NAME="A342C970d0"></A>A Simple Lighting Calculation </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80402mhay"></A>The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder1_c.html#Ggi2e0marj">cylinder1.c</A></B>
example program (found in Symbol.&amp;TRGraphics;) illustrates how to use
GL to light a cylinder using a simple lighting calculation. Consider a
pale gray cylinder with a rough surface that is illuminated by a source
of white light. Objects with rough surfaces tend to reflect or scatter
light equally in all directions. Such reflections are termed diffuse reflections.</P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80422mhay"></A>In our simple lighting calculation, the
color and intensity of the diffusely reflected light at a point on the
surface depends on three things: </P>


<UL><LI><A NAME="A342C970d3"></A>Light source color</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C970d4"></A>The angular relationship between the light
source direction and reflecting surface orientation at that point</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C970d5"></A>The reflectance characteristics of the cylinder
surface</LI></UL>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80445mhay"></A>The short arrows in the following <A HREF="figures/gl32p23.jpg">figure</A>
show how the diffuse light is scattered equally in all directions. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80467mhay"></A>The orientation of the reflecting surface
is specified by the surface normal vector, which is perpendicular to the
surface at the point in question. The normal vector must be normalized
(must be of unit length). Because the surface normal differs at every point
on a curved surface, the calculation for reflected light produces a different
color at every point on the surface. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80488mhay"></A>The number of points used in the lighting
calculations depends on the number of vertices used to define the surface.
For a local light (a light not very far from the surface), the system computes
a color at every vertex of the polygon mesh used to represent the surface.
The application writer must specify the surface-normal vector at every
vertex of the polygon mesh. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80509mhay"></A>In addition to the light originating from
the light source that reflects off the surface, ambient light is also accounted for in the model. Ambient light is assumed
to be nondirectional and is reflected uniformly in all directions by the
reflecting surface. Thus, the color and intensity of the reflected ambient
light are functions of both the level of ambient light in the scene and
the reflectance properties of the surface. They are not functions of the
angular relationship between the source of light and the surface normal.</P>


<H4><A NAME="A258C01bfc2"></A>Subroutines from Example Program cylinder1.c</H4>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80531mhay"></A>The example C language program <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder1_c.html#Ggi2e0marj">cylinder1.c</A></B>
introduces four new subroutines that use the GL lighting facility. The
new subroutines are <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/mmode.html#XhZ2370marj">mmode</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmbind.html#XeZ2340marj">lmbind</A></B>,
and <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/n3f.html#A139X91ef3">n3f</A></B>.</P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80552mhay"></A>To perform lighting calculations, the
system must be able to distinguish between the projection matrix (used
by the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/perspective.html#A144X94da">perspective</A></B>
subroutine) and the viewing and modeling matrix (used by the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lookat.html#A144X9452">lookat</A></B>
subroutine and the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/rotate.html#A8g2120marj">rotate</A></B>
subroutine). The <B>mmode</B> subroutine is used to indicate to the hardware
which matrices represent <A HREF="specialterms.html#A27P021">projection transformations</A>
and which represent <A HREF="specialterms.html#A27P021">viewing</A> or <A HREF="specialterms.html#A27P021">modeling
transformation</A>s. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80573mhay"></A>The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine, called from the <TT><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder1_c.html#A64EA57551ttay">def_simple_light_calc</A></TT> subroutine of the example program, found
in  in<I> GL3.2 Version 4 for AIX: Graphics Library (GL) Technical Reference</I>, defines instances of the three necessary components
to perform a lighting calculation: </P>


<UL><LI><A NAME="A342C970dc"></A>A surface material</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C970dd"></A>A light source</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C970de"></A>A lighting model</LI></UL>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80597mhay"></A>The program line <TT>lmdef(DEFMATERIAL,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;NULL)</TT>
tells GL about surface material number 1. The value given the first parameter,
<TT>DEFMATERIAL</TT>, indicates that you are defining a surface material.
The value for the second parameter defines this material as material number
<TT>1</TT>. The value for the third parameter (<TT>0</TT>) is the length
of the properties array specified by the fourth parameter. The properties
array specifies the properties of the surface material. Here, NULL instructs
GL to use the default values for surface materials. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80619mhay"></A>The next two calls to the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine are similar to the first. By substituting <TT>DEFMATERIAL</TT>
with <TT>DEFLIGHT,</TT> and subsequently <TT>DEFLMODEL</TT>, you can define
a light source and lighting model using the default values prescribed by
GL. The default values for a surface material, a light source, and a lighting
model are all that are necessary to perform a simple lighting calculation.
Properties of a lighting model are the properties that affect the entire
scene rather than a specific light source or surface material (the intensity
and color of the ambient light in the scene). The subroutine <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
is covered in greater detail in the section on <A HREF="lightsubs.html#lightsubs.html">lighting
subroutines</A>. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80641mhay"></A>Another subroutine introduced in the example
program is the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmbind.html#XeZ2340marj">lmbind</A></B>
subroutine. Once you have defined a surface material, light source, and
lighting model you can instruct GL to use them when performing lighting
calculations. The three calls to the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmbind.html#XeZ2340marj">lmbind</A></B>
subroutine in the example program tell the system to use the material,
light source, and light model defined by the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80663mhay"></A>It is more efficient to define surface
materials, light sources, and lighting models before activating them with
the <B>lmbind</B> subroutine because more computation is involved in defining
models than in invoking them. By predefining all the materials, light sources,
and lighting models to use in your application, you can quickly switch
among different materials and lighting sources when drawing a scene. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80684mhay"></A>There can be only one active light model
and surface material at any one time. However, you can use up to the value
of MAXLIGHTS lights, where MAXLIGHTS is a constant defined in the <B>/usr/include/gl/gl.h</B>
file. (The value is 8 for the High Performance 3-D Color Graphics Processor,
and should not be changed.) The example program <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder2_c.html#A16C0c87c">cylinder2.c</A></B>
(found in  in<I> GL3.2 Version 4 for AIX: Graphics Library (GL) Technical Reference</I>) uses multiple lights. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80706mhay"></A>The final new subroutine is the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/n3f.html#A139X91ef3">n3f</A></B>
subroutine. Use it to define surface normal vectors. Look at the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/n3f.html#A139X91ef3">n3f</A></B>
subroutine called from the 
<TT><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder1_c.html#A64EA59429ttay">draw_cylinder</A></TT> subroutine of the example program (found
in  in<I> GL3.2 Version 4 for AIX: Graphics Library (GL) Technical Reference</I>) . In the simple lighting calculation, the resultant
color at a vertex depends on the angular relationship between the surface
normal at that vertex and the light source direction. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80728mhay"></A>The call to the <B>n3f</B> subroutine
sends a normal vector of unit length to the graphics hardware to be transformed
and subsequently used for a lighting calculation. Each time a different
normal is sent to the graphics hardware, a lighting calculation is performed
and the resultant color is associated with the vertex (using the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/v.html#A144X97a4">v3f</A></B>
subroutine) following the <B>n3f</B> command. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80749mhay"></A>If you have not done so already, try running
the example program <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder1_c.html#Ggi2e0marj">cylinder1.c</A></B>.
Notice as the cylinder rotates, the color changes to different shades of
gray. This is because the angular relationships between the surface normals
and the light source (which happens to be located behind our eye along
the <I>z</I> axis) is changing. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80771mhay"></A>Also, note that as the interior of the
cylinder comes into view, the interior color appears a constant shade of
dark gray. This is because the surface normals are facing away from the
light source, so the interior of the cylinder is illuminated only by ambient
light, which is independent of the direction of the light source. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80792mhay"></A>Now that you have seen how to implement
a simple lighting calculation, you can expand the capabilities of the lighting
calculation to include specularity and multiple surface materials and lights.</P>


<H3><A NAME="A342C970eb"></A>Specularity<A NAME="INDEX502"></A> <A NAME="INDEX503"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX504"></A> <A NAME="INDEX505"></A> </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80814mhay"></A>What if the cylinder in the example were
made of a shiny metal instead of a rough material? Compared to rough or
diffusely reflecting surfaces that reflect light equally in all directions,
smooth surfaces tend to reflect light in a directional manner. This directional
reflection, called specular reflection, is what causes highlights. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80836mhay"></A>On a perfectly smooth surface such as
a mirror, the direction of a reflected ray is equal to the angle of incidence
(that is, the angle between the light direction vector and the surface
normal vector). On surfaces that are less than perfectly smooth there will
be some scattering of the reflected light. Thus, the angle of the reflected
light is weighted towards, but not always equal to, the angle of incidence
(see the following <A HREF="figures/gl32p24.jpg">figure</A>). </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80858mhay"></A>Calculations for diffusely reflected light
from a light source depend on the angular relationship between the surface
normal and light source direction, as well as the reflectance characteristics
of the surface. In addition to reflectance characteristics, specularly
reflected light depends on the angular relationships between the surface
normal, light source direction, and view direction. When the view direction
coincides with the direction of the reflected light rays, the viewer sees
a specular highlight or glare. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80880mhay"></A>The surface material of the cylinder can
be made to appear smoother by incorporating specular reflections. You can
do this by changing the <TT><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder1_c.html#A64EA57551ttay">def_simple_light_calc</A></TT> subroutine to look like this: </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C970f2"></A>def_simple_light_model(){</PRE>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C970f4"></A>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;lmdef(DEFMATERIAL,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;11,&nbsp;shiny_material);
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;lmdef(DEFLIGHT,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;NULL);
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;lmdef(DEFLMODEL,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;NULL);
}</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80904mhay"></A>At the module level of the program, include
the definition for the <TT>shiny_material</TT> property array: </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C970f9"></A>float&nbsp;&nbsp;shiny_material[]&nbsp;=&nbsp;{
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;SPECULAR,&nbsp;0.8,&nbsp;0.8,&nbsp;0.8,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;DIFFUSE,&nbsp;0.4,&nbsp;0.4,&nbsp;0.4,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;SHININESS,&nbsp;30.0,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;LMNULL};</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80926mhay"></A>Now we have provided a non-<TT>NULL</TT>
properties array; values are available for further lighting calculations.
Properties are set by specifying a property identifier followed by the
expected values for that property. In our example, we set the specular
reflectance (using <TT>SPECULAR</TT> as the property identifier) of the
surface for the red, green, and blue components of white light to <TT>[0.8</TT>,
<TT>0.8</TT>, and <TT>0.8],</TT> respectively. Likewise, the diffuse reflectance
was set to <TT>[0.4</TT>, <TT>0.4</TT>, <TT>0.4]</TT>. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80948mhay"></A>Reflectance components vary between 0.0
and 1.0 (0.0 being 0% reflective and 1.0 being 100% reflective). The shininess
property indicates how smooth or shiny the surface appears. The higher
the number, the smoother the surface, and subsequently the more focused
the specular highlight. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80969mhay"></A>The values for <TT>SHININESS</TT> can
range from <TT>0.0</TT> (no specular highlight) to <TT>128.0</TT> (very
focused specular highlight). The shininess specified should be a whole
number. When a property identifier and the corresponding values are specified
in a call to the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine, the new value for that property overrides a default that is
provided by GL. This way, you have to specify only those properties whose
default values you do not want. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80991mhay"></A>You must always end a property list with
the <TT>LMNULL</TT> token. This token lets GL know that you are finished
specifying properties. There are more properties for surface materials
that we have not discussed as well as other properties that apply specifically
to lighting models and light sources. A complete description of all the
properties available to the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine call and their defaults appears in the section on <A HREF="lightsubs.html#lightsubs.html">Lighting
Subroutines</A> . </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81012mhay"></A>If you run the example program with these
changes, you will notice how much shinier the cylinder looks. Watch how
the highlight appears when the surface normals point at your eye and disappear
as they move away. </P>


<H3><A NAME="A342C97101"></A>Multiple Surface Materials and Multiple Lights<A NAME="INDEX506"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX507"></A> <A NAME="INDEX508"></A> <A NAME="INDEX509"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX510"></A> <A NAME="INDEX511"></A> <A NAME="INDEX512"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX513"></A> <A NAME="INDEX514"></A> <A NAME="INDEX515"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX516"></A> <A NAME="INDEX517"></A> </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81035mhay"></A>The next example program displays two
intersecting cylinders, using a different surface material for each cylinder.
You can also light each cylinder with two light sources. Study the example
program <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder2_c.html#A16C0c87c">cylinder2.c</A></B>
(found in  in<I> GL3.2 Version 4 for AIX: Graphics Library (GL) Technical Reference</I>) . </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81057mhay"></A>At the top of the program, a second property
list is defined for a new material called <TT>purple_material</TT> and
a property list for a second light called <TT>blue_light</TT>. In the <TT>blue_light</TT>
property list, the light direction is specified as <TT>[0.0,&nbsp;1.0,&nbsp;0.0,&nbsp;0.0</TT>].
The first three numbers specify the <I>xyz</I> direction of the light.
The direction vector <TT>[0.0,&nbsp;1.0,&nbsp;0.0]</TT> indicates that
the light direction is along the <I>y</I> axis pointing towards the origin.</P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81079mhay"></A>In other words, the blue light is above
the cylinders and pointing toward them. The fourth number (<TT>0.0</TT>)
indicates that the light is positioned infinitely far away along the direction
vector (in our example the <I>y</I> axis). Differences between infinite
and noninfinite lights are discussed in <A HREF="advlightcap.html#advlightcap.html">&quot;Advanced
Lighting Capabilities&quot;</A>. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81101mhay"></A>The <TT>LCOLOR</TT> specifies the RGB
color of the light. This light has only blue color. By varying the values
of each of the three color components between 0.0 and 1.0 you can vary
the intensity of the light. That is, setting the blue light color to <TT>[0.0,&nbsp;0.0,&nbsp;0.6]</TT>
produces a more intense blue than it would have been if you had set the
color to <TT>[0.0,&nbsp;0.0,&nbsp;0.3</TT>]. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81123mhay"></A>In the <TT><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder2_c.html#A64EA47488ttay">def_light_calc</A></TT> subroutine, additional material and light
source are defined using the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine. In the <TT><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder2_c.html#A64EA47742ttay">use_light_calc</A></TT> portion of the program, both light sources
are bound because both are used during the entire animation. However, because
you want to switch back and forth between surface materials, the program
does not bind the surface material until ready to use it. In the main loop,
the program performs an </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C971d0"></A>lmbind(MATERIAL,&nbsp;1)</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81145mhay"></A>before drawing the first cylinder and
then another </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C971d2"></A>lmbind(MATERIAL,&nbsp;2)</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81167mhay"></A>when drawing the second cylinder. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81188mhay"></A>When you run the example program <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder2_c.html#A16C0c87c">cylinder2.c</A></B>,
notice that the first cylinder has the same surface material as the cylinder
drawn by the example program <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/cylinder1_c.html#Ggi2e0marj">cylinder1.c</A></B>,
but that the second cylinder consists of a duller, purple material. In
addition, each cylinder reflects different amounts of the blue overhead
light. </P>




<hr><center>
```

## File: gl32prgd/lightexec.html
```html
<!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD HTML 3.2//EN">
<HTML>

<!--gl32prgd/lightexec.html Mon, 24 Jan 2022 16:28:09 GMT -->
<HEAD>
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=iso-8859-1">

<TITLE>Lighting Execution Time and Performance
</TITLE>
</HEAD>

<body bgcolor="#fcfbf0">
<center>
[  <a href="lightsubs.html">Previous</a>  |
<a href="lightformula.html">Next</a>  |
<A HREF="toc.html" TARGET="_parent">Contents</A>  
 <A HREF="../gl32prgd/specialterms.html" TARGET="_parent">| Glossary</A>  
 <A HREF="topnav/topnav.html" TARGET="_top"></A>  
 <A HREF="cgi-bin/ds_form?config=/usr/share/man/info/en_US/a_doc_lib/data/base.cfg" TARGET="_top"></A>  ]
<hr>
<font color="#a62a2a" size="+2">
<i>GL3.2 Version 4.1 for AIX: Programming Concepts</i></font>
</center>
<hr size=3 noshade>
<H2><A NAME="lightexec.html"></A>Lighting Execution Time and Performance</H2>
<A NAME="INDEX571" REL="I1" TITLE="GL"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX572" REL="I2" TITLE="lighting effects"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX573" REL="I3" TITLE="execution time"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX574" REL="I1" TITLE="lighting effects"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX575" REL="I2" TITLE="GL"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX576" REL="I3" TITLE="execution time"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX577" REL="I1" TITLE="lighting effects"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX578" REL="I2" TITLE="GL"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX579" REL="I3" TITLE="performance"></A>
<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83138mhay"></A>The lighting equation is evaluated whenever the normal or the graphics position changes, depending on whether the viewer and light sources are local. If the viewer is local, or any of the light sources are local, then the lighting calculation is performed when the graphics position changes (for example, when a <!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/v.html#A144X97a4"><B>v3f</B></A> command is issued).</P>

<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83159mhay"></A>When the viewer is local, the vector from the vertex to the eye is different for each vertex and has to be calculated for each point. If the viewer is at infinity, then view vector is constant for all vertices and the calculation time is less. When a light source is local, the vector from the vertex to the light source is different for each vertex and has to be calculated for each vertex. If a light is at infinity, then light direction vector is constant for all vertices and the calculation time is less.</P>

<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83179mhay"></A>Performance is highest when an infinite viewer and a single infinite light source are used in the lighting calculation. Execution time increases slightly for each infinite light source added to the computation. However, the addition of local light sources increases the execution time noticeably.</P>

<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83200mhay"></A>After a normal is transformed by the inverse transpose of the modeling/viewing matrix, it must be renormalized if the transforming matrix is not orthonormal. This renormalization takes additional time and results in lower performance.</P>

<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83220mhay"></A>A matrix is orthonormal if each of its row vectors is of unit length and orthogonal to the others. Rotations and translations are always orthonormal. Shear transformations are never orthonormal. Because GL does not have any built-in shear transformations, the only transformations that might generate a nonorthonormal modeling/viewing matrix are the <!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/multmatrix.html#A144X9474"><B>multmatrix</B></A> and <!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/loadmatrix.html#A144X9430"><B>loadmatrix</B></A> subroutines, and the <!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/scale.html#A144X95a6"><B>scale</B></A> subroutine when the <I>x</I>, <I>y</I>, and <I>z</I> scale factors are not equal. </P>

<BLOCKQUOTE><A NAME="A33C0117e9"></A><B>Note: </B>If the transformation has been made nonorthonormal by introducing a shear or other nonorthonormal transformation, the system is automatically renormalizing normal vectors. In such a case, you do not need to feed normalized normal vectors to the system because they are renormalized anyway. Note, however, this should not be used as a trick to avoid explicit normalization by the user application.</BLOCKQUOTE>

<hr><center>
[  <a href="lightsubs.html">Previous</a>  |
<a href="lightformula.html">Next</a>  |

</center></BODY>
```

```html
<HEAD>
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=iso-8859-1">

<TITLE>Lighting Introduction
</TITLE>
</HEAD>

<body bgcolor="#fcfbf0">
<center>
[  <a href="listlightsubs.html">Previous</a>  |
<a href="lightbasics.html">Next</a>  |
<A HREF="toc.html" TARGET="_parent">Contents</A>  
 <A HREF="../gl32prgd/specialterms.html" TARGET="_parent">| Glossary</A>  
 <A HREF="topnav/topnav.html" TARGET="_top"></A>  
 <A HREF="cgi-bin/ds_form?config=/usr/share/man/info/en_US/a_doc_lib/data/base.cfg" TARGET="_top"></A>  ]
<hr>
<font color="#a62a2a" size="+2">
<i>GL3.2 Version 4.1 for AIX: Programming Concepts</i></font>
</center>
<hr size=3 noshade>
<H2><A NAME="lightintro.html"></A>Lighting Introduction</H2>
<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80291mhay"></A>The GL lighting model facility automatically calculates color using the geometries, colors, and properties of the currently bound material, lights, and lighting model. The lighting model subroutines can define multiple materials, lights, and lighting models. A lighting equation consists of one material, eight lights, and one lighting model.</P>

<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80312mhay"></A>A significant feature of GL is that the hardware can efficiently perform the lighting calculations needed to enhance the realism of the displayed geometry. Because different applications require different degrees of realism, the lighting facility in GL provides a variety of capabilities and features that allow you to control the degree of realism in the images produced by your application. You can use many of these realism features without a negative effect on the drawing performance.</P>

<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80332mhay"></A>When you look at an object in the real world, the color of that object (as perceived by your eye) depends on several parameters:</P>

<UL><LI><A NAME="A342C970cb"></A>The color, location, and direction of the light source or sources illuminating the object.</LI>

<LI><A NAME="A342C970cc"></A>The color and surface properties of the object itself.</LI>

<LI><A NAME="A342C970cd"></A>The position and view direction of the observer.</LI></UL>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA80356mhay"></A>Although GL allows you to control all of these parameters, you will find that you can produce quite realistic images by using only a subset of the available parameters.</P><hr><center>
[  <a href="listlightsubs.html">Previous</a>  |
<a href="lightbasics.html">Next</a>  |
<A HREF="toc.html" TARGET="_parent">Contents</A>  
 <A HREF="../gl32prgd/specialterms.html" TARGET="_parent">| Glossary</A>  
 <A HREF="topnav/topnav.html" TARGET="_top"></A>  
 <A HREF="cgi-bin/ds_form?config=/usr/share/man/info/en_US/a_doc_lib/data/base.cfg" TARGET="_top"></A>  ]
</center></BODY>


<!--gl32prgd/lightintro.html Mon, 24 Jan 2022 16:28:07 GMT -->
</HTML>
```

## File: gl32prgd/lightmatrix.html
```html
<!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD HTML 3.2//EN">
<HTML>

<!--gl32prgd/lightmatrix.html Mon, 24 Jan 2022 16:28:08 GMT -->
<HEAD>
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=iso-8859-1">

   <TITLE>Lighting in Matrix Mode
</TITLE>
   
</HEAD>

<body bgcolor="#fcfbf0">
<center>
[  <a href="advlightcap.html">Previous</a>  |
<a href="lightsubs.html">Next</a>  |
<A HREF="toc.html" TARGET="_parent">Contents</A>  
 <A HREF="../gl32prgd/specialterms.html" TARGET="_parent">| Glossary</A>  
 <A HREF="topnav/topnav.html" TARGET="_top"></A>  
 <A HREF="cgi-bin/ds_form?config=/usr/share/man/info/en_US/a_doc_lib/data/base.cfg" TARGET="_top"></A>  ]
<hr>
<font color="#a62a2a" size="+2">
<i>GL3.2 Version 4.1 for AIX: Programming Concepts</i></font>
</center>
<hr size=3 noshade>



<H2><A NAME="lightmatrix.html"></A>Lighting in Matrix Mode </H2>


<P><A NAME="INDEX554"></A><A NAME="INDEX555"></A><A NAME="INDEX556"></A><A NAME="INDEX557"></A><A NAME="INDEX558"></A><A NAME="INDEX559"></A><A NAME="INDEX560"></A><A NAME="INDEX561"></A></P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81894mhay"></A>This section outlines the technique of
creating lighting effects in matrix mode: </P>


<UL><LI><A NAME="A258C01bfd8"></A><A HREF="lightmatrix.html#FPL220marj">Transforming
Vectors</A> into Normalized Device Coordinates</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A258C01bfd9"></A><A HREF="lightmatrix.html#A342C9733a">Positioning
the Lights</A></LI></UL>


<H3><A NAME="FPL220marj"></A>Transforming Vectors into Normalized Device
Coordinates </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81918mhay"></A>If you are not doing lighting calculations,
the geometric transformation pipeline is relatively simple. Vertices (vectors)
representing positions in 3-D space are transformed into normalized device
coordinates (NDCs, that is, 3-D cubes whose <I>x</I>, <I>y</I>, and <I>z</I>
coordinates are restricted to lie between -1.0 and 1.0) and then scaled
to the physical window (and screen) integer coordinates. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81939mhay"></A>The transformation to NDCs is accomplished
by multiplying the input vector by a matrix that represents the combined
actions of modeling, viewing, and <A HREF="coordtransfrms.html#A264X9141">projection
transformations</A>. Each of the individual transformations is represented
by a matrix, and these can all be multiplied together to yield one matrix
that has the same effect as the sequential application of all the individual
matrices. (See <A HREF="workcoords.html#workcoords.html">&quot;Working with
Coordinate Systems&quot;</A>for more information.) </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81960mhay"></A>For lighting calculations, the transformation
is done in two steps because the calculations require vectors transformed
by the modeling and viewing matrices but not yet projected. The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/mmode.html#XhZ2370marj">mmode</A></B>
subroutine is required to put the system into the two-step mode when lighting
is turned on. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA81981mhay"></A>In the one-step mode, all transformations
are kept on one transformation stack, and all transformation subroutines
operate on that stack. In the two-step mode, modeling/viewing transformations
are kept separate from the projection transformations. The modeling/viewing
transformations are kept on a stack; the projection matrix is kept separately
and is not on a stack. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82002mhay"></A>There are three matrix modes: MSINGLE,
MVIEWING, and MPROJECTION. The default is MSINGLE, the one-step mode. The
system can be placed in the one-step mode by calling </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A34C011a70"></A>mmode(MSINGLE);</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82024mhay"></A>although, by default, it is already in
that mode. To use lighting the system MUST be placed in the MVIEWING mode.
This is done by making the call </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C97328"></A>mmode(MVIEWING);</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82046mhay"></A>After this call, all matrix subroutines
operate on the matrix stack. The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/getmatrix.html#A144X940e">getmatrix</A></B>
subroutine returns the top matrix on the modeling/viewing stack; the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/loadmatrix.html#A144X9430">loadmatrix</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/multmatrix.html#A144X9474">multmatrix</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/rotate.html#A8g2120marj">rotate</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/translate.html#A144X95c8">translate</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/scale.html#A144X95a6">scale</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lookat.html#A144X9452">lookat</A></B>,
and <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/polarview.html#A144X94fc">polarview</A></B>
all operate on the top matrix of the stack. Note, however, that the perspective
projection subroutines (<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/perspective.html#A144X94da">perspective</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/window.html#A144X95ea">window</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/ortho.html#A144X9496">ortho2</A></B>,
or <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/ortho.html#A144X9496">ortho</A></B>)
are an exception: they do <I>not</I> operate on the modeling/viewing stack,
but rather affect the projection matrix directly. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82068mhay"></A>If the application needs to define a customized
perspective transformation (one that is not covered by <B>perspective,
window, ortho</B>, or <B>ortho2</B>) while lighting is turned on, the application
should go into MPROJECTION mode by calling </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C9732f"></A>mmode(MPROJECTION);</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82092mhay"></A>In this mode all the matrix subroutines
operate on the projection matrix. The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/getmatrix.html#A144X940e">getmatrix</A></B>
subroutine returns the current projection matrix. The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/loadmatrix.html#A144X9430">loadmatrix</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/multmatrix.html#A144X9474">multmatrix</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/rot.html#A144X9562">rot</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/rotate.html#A8g2120marj">rotate</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/translate.html#A144X95c8">translate</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/scale.html#A144X95a6">scale</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lookat.html#A144X9452">lookat</A></B>,
and <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/polarview.html#A144X94fc">polarview</A></B>
all operate directly on the projection matrix, as well as the usual projection
subroutines (<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/perspective.html#A144X94da">perspective</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/window.html#A144X95ea">window</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/ortho.html#A144X9496">ortho2</A></B>,
and <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/ortho.html#A144X9496">ortho</A></B>).
On the other hand, the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/pushmatrix.html#A144X9540">pushmatrix</A></B>
and <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/popmatrix.html#A144X951e">popmatrix</A></B>
calls make no sense in this mode because the stack is not directly accessible.
Furthermore, no drawing should be done while in MPROJECTION mode; the system
is not configured for drawing when it is in this mode. When you are finished
defining the projection matrix, you should go back directly to MVIEWING
mode. Please heed the following note of caution: </P>


<BLOCKQUOTE><P><A NAME="A34C011a75"></A><B>Attention: </B>Entering or leaving MSINGLE
mode scrambles the contents of the matrix stack and leaves the current
projection matrix undefined. </P></BLOCKQUOTE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82115mhay"></A>When you write a GL program, you must
always remember to initialize the transformations. By default, they are
NOT pre-initialized by the system. In the one-step mode (MSINGLE mode),
a call to <B>loadmatrix</B> or to one of the four projection subroutines
(<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/perspective.html#A144X94da">perspective</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/window.html#A144X95ea">window</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/ortho.html#A144X9496">ortho2</A></B>,
or <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/ortho.html#A144X9496">ortho</A></B>)
is sufficient. In the two-step mode, both the projection and the modeling/viewing
matrices must be initialized. Again, calls to the projection subroutines
are sufficient to initialize the projection matrix; the modeling/viewing
matrix can be initialized by a call to the <B>loadmatrix</B> subroutine
while in MVIEWING mode. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82136mhay"></A>Normally, you load the identity matrix
(a 4x4 matrix with ones running along the diagonal, the other entries zero),
although any matrix may be loaded. The initialization is required because
most of the matrix subroutines (<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/multmatrix.html#A144X9474">multmatrix</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/rot.html#A144X9562">rot</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/rotate.html#A8g2120marj">rotate</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/translate.html#A144X95c8">translate</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/scale.html#A144X95a6">scale</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lookat.html#A144X9452">lookat</A></B>,
and <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/polarview.html#A144X94fc">polarview</A></B>
) multiply into the current matrix, and if that matrix does not exist,
the multiplication cannot take place. Remember, if you intend to use lighting,
you must leave MSINGLE mode before performing the initialization. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82157mhay"></A>Like vertices, normal vectors associated
with the vertices must also be transformed. However, normals are transformed
according to different mathematical rules than vertices. For lighting calculations,
the normal vectors are multiplied by the inverse transpose of the 3X3 upper
left submatrix of the modeling/viewing transformation. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82178mhay"></A>As you operate on the modeling/viewing
stack, its inverse transpose is automatically kept up to date. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82199mhay"></A>The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/getmmode.html#idZ2e0marj">getmmode</A></B>
subroutine returns the current matrix mode. The values returned can be
compared to the values of MSINGLE, MPROJECTION, and MVIEWING to determine
the current mode. Mode identifiers are defined in the <B>/usr/include/gl/gl.h</B>file. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82219mhay"></A>The following <A HREF="figures/gl32p26.jpg">figure</A>
illustrates the calculations done to each vertex sent down the pipeline
in MVIEWING mode. </P>


<H3><A NAME="A342C9733a"></A>Positioning the Lights </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82242mhay"></A>When a light is bound with the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmbind.html#XeZ2340marj">lmbind</A></B>
subroutine, the location it takes up in world space depends on the transformation
on the top of the matrix stack. That is, the coordinates of the light are
run through the geometry pipeline just as any other 3-D coordinate would
be. This must be kept in mind when rendering complex, animated scenes.</P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82264mhay"></A>How to draw a scene where the eyepoint
changes from frame to frame, while the light remains fixed in world coordinates,
or to draw a scene where the light moves about from frame to frame, might
not be immediately obvious. Therefore, we summarize the following steps
to achieve a moving eyepoint and/or to have moving lights. There are five
general cases: </P>


<UL><LI><A NAME="A342C9733c"></A>A static eyepoint and a static light.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C9733d"></A>A static eyepoint and a moving light.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C9733e"></A>A moving eyepoint and a static light.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C9733f"></A>A moving eyepoint and a moving light.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C97340"></A>A moving eyepoint with the light attached
to the eyepoint.</LI></UL>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82289mhay"></A>The general rules for binding lights are:</P>


<UL><LI><A NAME="A342C97342"></A>Call <TT>lmbind(LIGHT#,&nbsp;index</TT>) after
changing the view.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C97343"></A>Call <TT>lmbind(LIGHT#,&nbsp;index</TT>) only
when transformations for the light are premultiplied on the stack.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C97344"></A>Never call <TT>lmbind(LIGHT#,&nbsp;index)</TT>
when transformations for surfaces are premultiplied on the stack.</LI></UL>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82313mhay"></A>The detailed steps in setting up the viewing
transformations, the modeling transformation, and the lighting model specifications
for each of these five cases are outlined here. The first four cases all
use the following pseudocode: </P>


<OL><LI><A NAME="A342C97347"></A>Specify the <A HREF="coordtransfrms.html#A264X915f">viewing
transformation</A>.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C01163f"></A>Push the transformation stack.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C011640"></A>Set up the modeling matrix to position the
light correctly.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C011641"></A>Call the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmbind.html#XeZ2340marj">lmbind</A></B>
subroutine to bind the light source.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C011642"></A>Pop the transformation stack.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C011643"></A>Push the transformation stack.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C011644"></A>Draw the objects.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C011645"></A>Pop the transformation stack.</LI></OL>


<H4><A NAME="A32C011646"></A>A Static Eyepoint and a Static Light </H4>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82343mhay"></A>In this scenario, the drawing loop simply
repeats steps 6 through 8. Presumably, the objects are drawn in different
locations each time through the loop, if you are interested in having moving
objects. </P>


<H4><A NAME="A342C9734b"></A>A Static Eyepoint and a Moving Light </H4>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82365mhay"></A>In this scenario, the drawing loop returns
to step 2 and repeats steps 2 through 8. Each time through the loop, change
the modeling transformation in step 3 to move the light. You can have either
moving or static objects by changing step 7. </P>


<H4><A NAME="A342C97354"></A>A Moving Eyepoint and a Static Light </H4>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82388mhay"></A>In this scenario, the drawing loop returns
to step 1 and repeats steps 1 through 8. Each time through the loop, change
the viewing transformation in step 1 to move the eyepoint. Do not change
the modeling matrix in step 3 if you do not want the light to move around
in world coordinates. Again, you can have either moving or static objects
by changing step&nbsp;7. </P>


<H4><A NAME="A342C9735b"></A>A Moving Eyepoint and a Moving Light </H4>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82410mhay"></A>In this scenario, the drawing loop returns
to step 1 and repeats steps 1 through 8. Each time through the loop, change
the viewing transformation in step 1 to move the eyepoint. Change the modeling
matrix in step 3 to move the light around. Again, you can have either moving
or static objects by changing step 7. </P>


<H4><A NAME="A342C97365"></A>A Moving Eyepoint with the Light Attached
to the Eyepoint </H4>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82432mhay"></A>This scenario requires a different sequence
of steps: </P>


<OL><LI><A NAME="A342C97366"></A>Specify the <A HREF="coordtransfrms.html#A264X915f">viewing
transformation</A>.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C01164c"></A>Set up the modeling matrix to position the
light correctly.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C97367"></A>Call the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmbind.html#XeZ2340marj">lmbind</A></B>
subroutine to bind the light source.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C97368"></A>Specify the viewing transformation again.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C01164d"></A>Push the transformation stack.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C97369"></A>Draw the objects.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A32C01164e"></A>Pop the transformation stack.</LI></OL>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82460mhay"></A>In this case, the drawing loop returns
to step 4 and repeats steps 4 through 7. Each time through the loop, change
the viewing transformation in step 4 to move the eyepoint. Again, you can
have either moving or static objects by changing step 6. </P>




<hr><center>
[  <a href="advlightcap.html">Previous</a>  |
<a href="lightsubs.html">Next</a>  |
<A HREF="toc.html" TARGET="_parent">Contents</A>  
 <A HREF="../gl32prgd/specialterms.html" TARGET="_parent">| Glossary</A>  
 <A HREF="topnav/topnav.html" TARGET="_top"></A>  
 <A HREF="cgi-bin/ds_form?config=/usr/share/man/info/en_US/a_doc_lib/data/base.cfg" TARGET="_top"></A>  ]
</center></BODY>


<!--gl32prgd/lightmatrix.html Mon, 24 Jan 2022 16:28:09 GMT -->
</HTML>
```

## File: gl32prgd/lightsubs.html
```html
<!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD HTML 3.2//EN">
<HTML>

<!--gl32prgd/lightsubs.html Mon, 24 Jan 2022 16:28:09 GMT -->

<H2><A NAME="lightsubs.html"></A>Lighting Subroutines </H2>


<P><A NAME="INDEX562"></A><A NAME="INDEX563"></A><A NAME="INDEX564"></A><A NAME="INDEX565"></A><A NAME="INDEX566"></A><A NAME="INDEX567"></A><A NAME="INDEX568"></A><A NAME="INDEX569"></A><A NAME="INDEX570"></A></P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82482mhay"></A>The GL lighting facility is implemented
with seven additional subroutines to the Graphics Library: </P>


<UL><LI><A NAME="A342C9736e"></A><B><A HREF="lightsubs.html#A354C9873f">n3f</A></B>
and <B><A HREF="lightsubs.html#A342C9737a">normal</A></B> subroutines,
which set the current normal.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C9736f"></A><B><A HREF="lightsubs.html#A342C97380">mmode</A></B>
subroutine, which sets the current matrix mode.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C97370"></A><B><A HREF="lightsubs.html#A342C9738d">getmmode</A></B>
subroutine, which returns the current matrix mode.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C97371"></A><B><A HREF="lightsubs.html#A342C97392">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine, which defines a material, light source, or lighting model.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A342C97372"></A><B><A HREF="lightsubs.html#A342C973d1">lmbind</A></B>
subroutine, which makes a material, light source, or lighting model current.</LI>


<LI><A NAME="A25C0f6d9"></A><B><A HREF="advlightcap.html#LuK21a0marj">lmcolor</A></B>
subroutine, which enables dynamic resetting of the material properties.</LI></UL>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82508mhay"></A>All lighting model property names and
constants are symbolically defined in the <B>/usr/include/gl/gl.h&nbsp;</B>file.</P>


<H3><A NAME="A354C9873f"></A>n3f Subroutine </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82531mhay"></A>The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/n3f.html#A139X91ef3">n3f</A></B>
subroutine takes the address of an array of three floating-point numbers
(the <I>vector</I> parameter) and sets the value for the current vertex
normal. Normal vectors are assumed to be of unit length, therefore, the
<A HREF="figures/gl32p27.jpg">equation</A> </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82552mhay"></A>should equal 1.0. The normal vector is
transformed into eye coordinates using the inverse transpose of the current
viewing matrix. It is then stored for use by the lighting equation. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82573mhay"></A>New normals can occur as frequently as
every new graphics position and as infrequently as desired. If only one
normal is given per polygon and the lighting equation is evaluated on a
per-normal basis (when using an infinite viewer and infinite light sources),
then the calculations are done only once per polygon. The syntax is as
follows: </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A258C01bfe2"></A>void&nbsp;n3f(Float32&nbsp;vector[3])</PRE>


<H3><A NAME="A342C9737a"></A>normal Subroutine </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82596mhay"></A>The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/normal.html#A142X9b7">normal</A></B>
subroutine takes exactly the same parameter as the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/n3f.html#A139X91ef3">n3f</A></B>
subroutine. The only difference is that <B>normal</B> can be used in display
lists and <B>n3f</B> cannot. The syntax is as follows: </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A258C01bfe3"></A>void&nbsp;normal(Coord&nbsp;narray[3])</PRE>


<H3><A NAME="A342C97380"></A>mmode Subroutine </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82619mhay"></A>The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/mmode.html#XhZ2370marj">mmode</A></B>
subroutine takes one integer parameter (<I>mode</I>), which is either MSINGLE,
MPROJECTION, or MVIEWING. The different modes are necessary to maintain
a separate projection matrix and a separate modeling/viewing matrix and
its inverse transpose. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82640mhay"></A>The modeling/viewing matrix transforms
model coordinates into eye coordinates where the lighting calculations
are performed. The inverse transpose of this matrix is used to transform
normals from model coordinates into eye coordinates. The projection matrix
transforms eye coordinates into screen coordinates. The figure entitled
<A HREF="figures/gl32p26.jpg">Lighting Calculations</A> shows how the various
matrices operate on display list coordinates and normal vectors to produce
screen coordinates and colors. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82661mhay"></A>The lighting equation uses output of the
modeling/viewing matrix and its inverse transpose. To use the lighting
facility, it is necessary to call <TT>mmode(MVIEWING)</TT> before setting
viewing or modeling matrices. This informs the system that future transformation
subroutines will affect the modeling/viewing matrix and its inverse transpose.
Each of the matrix modes is described fully in the following sections.
The syntax is as follows: </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A258C01bfe4"></A>void&nbsp;mmode(Int16&nbsp;mode)</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82683mhay"></A>MSINGLE mode is the default mode. The
viewing, modeling, and projection matrices are combined into one matrix,
which the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/getmatrix.html#A144X940e">getmatrix</A></B>
subroutine returns. Because all matrices are combined in MSINGLE mode,
there is no way to transform model coordinates into eye coordinates or
to transform normals. Therefore, the lighting model facility does not work
in MSINGLE mode. Entering or exiting from MSINGLE mode pops the entire
matrix stack and leaves the current matrix undefined. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82704mhay"></A>In MPROJECTION mode, all matrix subroutines
deal only with the projection matrix. There is only one projection matrix,
and the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/pushmatrix.html#A144X9540">pushmatrix</A></B>
and <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/popmatrix.html#A144X951e">popmatrix</A></B>
subroutines result in errors in MPROJECTION mode. The <B>getmatrix</B>
subroutine returns the current projection matrix. The modeling/viewing
matrix is disabled while in MPROJECTION mode: the results of transforming
points in MPROJECTION are undefined. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82725mhay"></A>In MVIEWING mode, all matrix subroutines
deal only with the modeling/viewing matrix and its inverse transpose. All
matrix subroutines premultiply or load the modeling/viewing matrix by the
matrix, and premultiply or load the inverse transpose viewing matrix with
the inverse transpose of the matrix. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82746mhay"></A>For the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/loadmatrix.html#A144X9430">loadmatrix</A></B>
and <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/multmatrix.html#A144X9474">multmatrix</A></B>
subroutines, the matrix has to be inverted, so singular matrices will cause
an error. In MVIEWING mode, the <B>getmatrix</B> subroutine returns the
modeling/viewing matrix. The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/perspective.html#A144X94da">perspective</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/window.html#A144X95ea">window</A></B>,
<B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/ortho.html#A144X9496">ortho</A></B>,
and <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/ortho.html#A144X9496">ortho2</A></B>
subroutines load a projection matrix even in <TT>MVIEWING</TT> mode. Because
these subroutines do not affect the modeling/viewing matrix stack and because
it is common to build a viewing matrix using subroutines that only multiply
matrices, it normally is necessary to load an identity matrix onto the
modeling/viewing matrix stack before defining the viewing matrix. </P>


<H3><A NAME="A342C9738d"></A>getmmode Subroutine </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82768mhay"></A>The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/getmmode.html#idZ2e0marj">getmmode</A></B>
subroutine returns the current matrix mode. The values returned can be
compared to the values of MSINGLE, MPROJECTION, and MVIEWING to determine
the current mode. Mode identifiers are defined in the <B>/usr/include/gl/gl.h</B>file. The syntax is as follows: </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A258C01bfe5"></A>Int32&nbsp;getmmode()</PRE>


<H3><A NAME="A342C97392"></A>lmdef Subroutine </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82791mhay"></A>The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine defines a new material, light source, or lighting model and
takes four parameters. The first parameter, <I>deftype</I>, specifies what
is to be defined and is either <TT>DEFMATERIAL</TT>, <TT>DEFLIGHT</TT>,
or <TT>DEFLMODEL</TT>. The second parameter, <I>index</I>, is the name
or index into the table of stored materials, light sources, or lighting
models. Indexes for each of these groups are independent. You can define
up to 65535 materials, 65535 light sources, and 65535 lighting models.
However, index 0 is predefined for each group and cannot be changed. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82812mhay"></A>The third parameter, <I>numpoints</I>,
is the length of the properties array and is the number of floating point
numbers contained within the array. The fourth parameter, <I>properties</I>,
is the properties array, which is a list of properties to be assigned to
the material, light source, or lighting model. Values in the array are
property identifiers, each followed by the appropriate number of data values.
All identifiers and data values are floating-point numbers. Only property
identifiers appropriate for the object being defined should be included
in the properties array. The last entry must be <TT>LMNULL (0.0)</TT>.
Property identifiers are defined in the <B>/usr/include/gl/gl.h </B>file.</P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82833mhay"></A>All properties have default values that
have been chosen for their efficient execution. The first time a material,
light, or lighting property is defined, it is initialized to the default
values. A definition can be set to all default values by calling the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine with either a null pointer to the property array (C programming
language only) or with <TT>LMNULL&nbsp;(0.0)</TT> as the first and only
property identifier. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82854mhay"></A>Incremental changes can be made to a material,
light source, or lighting model definition. Each call to the <B>lmdef</B>
subroutine changes only the properties included in its properties array.
Properties that are not specified in the properties array keep their previous
values. Any valid property can be changed regardless of whether that property
is relevant to the current lighting calculation. However, changes made
to a definition that is currently bound are effective immediately. </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82875mhay"></A>The format of the properties array is
a sequence of property identifiers each followed by the appropriate number
of data values. The last array entry must be LMNULL. Described below are
the material, light source, and lighting model properties along with the
number of data values that follow each identifier. Each property is called
by its symbolic name. The syntax is as follows: </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A258C01bfe6"></A>void&nbsp;lmdef(Int16&nbsp;deftype,&nbsp;Int32&nbsp;index,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Int16&nbsp;numpoints,&nbsp;Float32&nbsp;properties[])</PRE>


<H4><A NAME="A85C19d"></A>Material Properties </H4>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82898mhay"></A>Material properties are all the properties
a material groups together to define its surface characteristics, such
as diffuse reflectance and shininess. The available material properties
are as follows: </P>


<TABLE><TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973a6"></A>EMISSION </TD>


<TD>The EMISSION property is the emission color of the material. Following
the property identifier should be the new R, G, B color values where 0.0
&amp;le; R, G, B &amp;le; 1.0.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973a8"></A>AMBIENT </TD>


<TD>The AMBIENT property is the ambient reflectance of the material. Following
the property identifier should be the new R, G, B color values where 0.0
&amp;le; R, G, B &amp;le; 1.0.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973aa"></A>DIFFUSE </TD>


<TD>The DIFFUSE property is the diffuse reflectance of the material. Following
the property identifier should be the new R, G, B color values where 0.0
&amp;le; R, G, B &amp;le; 1.0.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973ac"></A>SPECULAR </TD>


<TD>The SPECULAR property is the specular reflectance of the material.
Following the property identifier should be the new R, G, B color values
where 0.0 &amp;le; R, G, B &amp;le; 1.0.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973ae"></A>SHININESS </TD>


<TD>The SHININESS property is the specular light scattering exponent. Following
the property identifier should be the new value for the shininess. The
values for shininess can range from 0.0 to 128.0 and should represent whole
numbers. If shininess &amp;le; 0.0 then there will be no specular highlight.
This is functionally equivalent to setting the material specular reflectance
to [0.0, 0.0, 0.0].</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A32C01164f"></A>ALPHA </TD>


<TD>The ALPHA property is the transparency of the material and can be used
when performing alpha blending. Following the property identifier should
be the new alpha value where 0.0 &amp;le; alpha &amp;le; 1.0. Certain alpha
blending operations require that alpha bitplanes be installed in the system.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A189C1103"></A>COLORINDEXES </TD>


<TD>Specifies the material properties used when lighting in color map mode.</TD></TR></TABLE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82926mhay"></A>The default values for material properties
are: </P>


<TABLE><TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117dd"></A>EMISSION </TD>


<TD>0.0, 0.0, 0.0</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117de"></A>AMBIENT </TD>


<TD>0.2, 0.2, 0.2</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117df"></A>DIFFUSE </TD>


<TD>0.8, 0.8, 0.8</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117e0"></A>SPECULAR </TD>


<TD>0.0, 0.0, 0.0</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117e1"></A>SHININESS </TD>


<TD>0.0</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A75C19"></A>ALPHA </TD>


<TD>1.0</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A189C1104"></A>COLORINDEXES </TD>


<TD>0.0, 127.5, 255.0</TD></TR></TABLE>


<H4><A NAME="A85C19e"></A>Light Source Properties </H4>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82955mhay"></A>Light source properties are all the properties
a light source groups together to define its characteristics, such as color
and position. The available light properties are as follows: </P>


<TABLE><TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973bd"></A>AMBIENT </TD>


<TD>The AMBIENT property is the color of the ambient light associated with
the light source. Following the property identifier should be the new R,
G, B color values where 0.0 &amp;le; R, G, B &amp;le; 1.0.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973bf"></A>LCOLOR </TD>


<TD>The LCOLOR property is the color of the light source. Following the
property identifier should be the new R, G, B color values where 0.0 &amp;le;
R, G, B &amp;le; 1.0.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973c1"></A>POSITION </TD>


<TD>The POSITION property is the position of the light source. Following
the property identifier should be the new <I>x</I>, <I>y</I>, <I>z</I>,
and <I>w</I> coordinates of the light. If the <I>w</I> coordinate of the
light source is 0.0, the light is an infinite light source and its position
specifies the light direction. (Such a light source can be called a directional
light source.) The light direction is computed by normalizing the light's
position vector. If the <I>w</I> coordinate of the light is not 0.0, then
the light is a local light and <I>x</I>, <I>y</I>, <I>z</I>, and <I>w</I>
are divided by <I>w</I> to specify the position. Light positions or directions
are defined in the current model coordinate space and are affected by the
current transformation matrix at the time they are bound.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A189C1105"></A>SPOTDIRECTION </TD>


<TD>Assigns the direction (axis) in which a spotlight source emits.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A189C1106"></A>SPOTLIGHT </TD>


<TD>Assigns the spread angle and concentration exponent of a spotlight.</TD></TR></TABLE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA82981mhay"></A>The default values for light source properties
are: </P>


<TABLE><TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117e2"></A>AMBIENT </TD>


<TD>0.0, 0.0, 0.0</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117e3"></A>LCOLOR </TD>


<TD>1.0, 1.0, 1.0</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117e4"></A>POSITION </TD>


<TD>0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A189C1107"></A>SPOTDIRECTION </TD>


<TD>0.0, 0.0, -1.0</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A189C1108"></A>SPOTLIGHT </TD>


<TD>0.0, 180.0</TD></TR></TABLE>


<H4><A NAME="A85C19f"></A>Lighting Model Properties </H4>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83008mhay"></A>Lighting model properties are all the
properties of a lighting model, such as scene ambient light and distance
attenuation factors. The available lighting model properties are as follows:</P>


<TABLE><TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973c8"></A>AMBIENT </TD>


<TD>The AMBIENT property is the color of ambient light in the scene. Following
the property identifier should be the new R, G, B color values where 0.0
&amp;le; R, G, B &amp;le; 1.0.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973ca"></A>LOCALVIEWER </TD>


<TD></TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP" COLSPAN="2">The LOCALVIEWER property informs the system whether
the viewer (eye position) is local to the scene. Following the property
identifier should be either 1.0 or 0.0 (true or false). If the viewer is
local, then the eye position is assumed to be located at (0,0,0) in eye
coordinates. When the viewer is local, the vector from the vertex to the
eye must be calculated for each vertex. If the viewer is not local, then
the viewer is at infinity along the positive <I>z</I> axis. The view direction
vector is [0,0,1] for all vertices. </TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</TD>


<TD><BLOCKQUOTE><P><A NAME="A169C12b6"></A><B>Note: </B>The LOCALVIEWER property affects
only the manner in which the lighting calculations are performed. The setting
of the LOCALVIEWER does not in any way affect the transformation stack
or alter the geometrical position of the surfaces being drawn. It only
affects their apparent color (the output of the lighting calculations).</P></BLOCKQUOTE></TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973cc"></A>ATTENUATION </TD>


<TD></TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP" COLSPAN="2">The ATTENUATION property is the scene attenuation
factors. Following the property identifier should be the new values for
the fixed scene attenuation factor and the variable scene attenuation factor.
If either factor is less than 0.0 then it is set to 0.0. If the variable
attenuation factor equals 0.0, then lighting attenuation is turned off.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</TD>


<TD></TD></TR></TABLE>


<P> </P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83033mhay"></A>The default values for lighting models
are: </P>


<TABLE><TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117e5"></A>AMBIENT </TD>


<TD>0.2, 0.2, 0.2 
<TABLE><TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117e6"></A>LOCALVIEWER </TD>


<TD>0.0</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A33C0117e7"></A>ATTENUATION </TD>


<TD>1.0, 0.0</TD></TR></TABLE>


<P> </P></TD></TR></TABLE>


<H3><A NAME="A342C973d1"></A>lmbind Subroutine </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83059mhay"></A>The <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmbind.html#XeZ2340marj">lmbind</A></B>
subroutine takes two integer parameters: the first, <I>target</I>, specifies
the target of the bind and the second, <I>index</I>, is the index of the
source. When a source is bound to a target, it becomes current and subsequent
evaluations of the lighting equation use its values. The syntax is as follows:</P>


<PRE><A NAME="A258C01bfe7"></A>void&nbsp;lmbind(Int16&nbsp;target,&nbsp;Int32&nbsp;index)</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83080mhay"></A>The three types of targets are as follows:</P>


<TABLE><TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973d9"></A>MATERIAL </TD>


<TD>If the target of a bind is MATERIAL, the source material becomes the
currently bound material. There is only one material target and therefore
only one currently bound material. 
<P><A NAME="A342C973da"></A>Source materials are specified using the same
index as when the material was defined using the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine. For example, </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C973db"></A>lmbind&nbsp;(MATERIAL,&nbsp;2)</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A342C973dc"></A>binds material definition 2 to the currently
bound material. Material 0 is the default material and disables lighting
calculations. This is the most efficient method to disable the lighting
calculations. It is functionally equivalent to binding lighting model 0.
If an undefined material is the source for the <B>lmbind</B> subroutine,
material 0 is bound instead. </P></TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973de"></A>LIGHTS </TD>


<TD>There are MAXLIGHTS lights available as targets (LIGHT0, LIGHT1, and
so on), and therefore a MAXLIGHTS number of current lights. If the target
of a bind is a light, then the source light replaces whatever light was
previously bound to the target. The replaced light is turned off and the
newly bound light is turned on. To turn a light off, bind light index 0
to the target light. 
<P><A NAME="A342C973df"></A>Source lights are specified using the same
index as when the light was defined using the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine. For example, </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C973e0"></A>lmbind&nbsp;(LIGHT3,&nbsp;54)</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A342C973e1"></A>binds user light definition 54 to system light
3. Light index 0 is the default light and while bound disables lighting
calculations for the system light target. If an undefined light is the
source to the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmbind.html#XeZ2340marj">lmbind</A></B>
subroutine, light 0 is bound instead. </P>


<P><A NAME="A342C973e2"></A>When a local light is bound, its position is
transformed by the current modeling/viewing matrix and stored. If the light
is infinite, its position is taken as its direction and is also transformed
by the current modeling/viewing matrix and stored. Thus, by binding a light
after some modeling transformations, a light can easily be made part of
an object that is moved through the scene (for example, a handheld candle).</P></TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP"><A NAME="A342C973e4"></A>LMODEL </TD>


<TD>If the target of a bind is LMODEL, then the source lighting model becomes
the current lighting model. There is only one lighting model target and
therefore only one current lighting model. 
<P><A NAME="A342C973e5"></A>Source lighting models are specified using
the same index as when the lighting model was defined using the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmdef.html#rgZ2250marj">lmdef</A></B>
subroutine. For example, </P>


<PRE><A NAME="A342C973e6"></A>lmbind&nbsp;(LMODEL,&nbsp;1)</PRE>


<P><A NAME="A342C973e7"></A>binds lighting model 1 to the current lighting
model. Lighting model 0 is the default lighting model and disables all
lighting calculations. If an undefined lighting model is the source for
the <B>lmbind</B> subroutine, lighting model 0 is bound instead. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>


<H3><A NAME="A32C011650"></A>lmcolor Subroutine </H3>


<P><A NAME="A3C0EA83117mhay"></A>The discussion of the <B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/lmcolor.html#ofZ220marj">lmcolor</A></B>
subroutine appears in <A HREF="advlightcap.html#advlightcap.html">&quot;Advanced
Lighting Capabilities&quot;</A>. </P>
```

```html
<hr>
<font color="#a62a2a" size="+2">
<i>GL3.2 Version 4.1 for AIX: Programming Concepts</i></font>
</center>
<hr size=3 noshade>
<H2><A NAME="linkncompil.html"></A>Linking and Compiling Using the GL Shared Library</H2>
<P><A NAME="A3C0F110692mhay"></A>The GL library <B>libgl.a</B> is a shared library. By default, a GL program linked with the <B>-lgl</B> flag will link to the <B>libgl.a</B> library as a shared library. By using shared libraries, programs minimize the amount of disk space and memory that they use. A shared library is not bound in with the executable; thus the size of the executable is smaller (kilobytes, for small programs, instead of megabytes). Memory usage is decreased, because several programs running at the same time share the .text segment (the segment where the executable code is contained) of the library (a separate .data segment is created for each program).</P>

<BLOCKQUOTE><A NAME="A6D93F6058vbia"></A><B>Attention: </B>The GL library cannot be linked non-shared. Doing so will result in erratic and incorrect behaviour of GL programs. This warning applies to the C version of GL (<B>libgl.a</B> library) as well as the FORTRAN version (<B>libfgl.a</B> library).</BLOCKQUOTE>

<hr><center>
```

```html
   <TITLE>Creating and Managing Windows in GL
</TITLE>
   
</HEAD>

<body bgcolor="#fcfbf0">
<center>
[  <a href="underwininput.html">Previous</a>  |
<a href="cursorgl.html">Next</a>  |
<A HREF="toc.html" TARGET="_parent">Contents</A>  
 <A HREF="../gl32prgd/specialterms.html" TARGET="_parent">| Glossary</A>  
 <A HREF="topnav/topnav.html" TARGET="_top"></A>  
 <A HREF="cgi-bin/ds_form?config=/usr/share/man/info/en_US/a_doc_lib/data/base.cfg" TARGET="_top"></A>  ]
<hr>
<font color="#a62a2a" size="+2">
<i>GL3.2 Version 4.1 for AIX: Programming Concepts</i></font>
</center>
<hr size=3 noshade>



<H2><A NAME="managewinds.html"></A>Creating and Managing Windows</H2>


<P><A NAME="INDEX766"></A><A NAME="INDEX767"></A><A NAME="INDEX768"></A><A NAME="INDEX769"></A><A NAME="INDEX770"></A><A NAME="INDEX771"></A></P>


<P><A NAME="A3C0ED56588mhay"></A>This section discusses the following aspects
of window management: </P>


<UL><LI><A NAME="A54C0149e8"></A><A HREF="managewinds.html#A44C012b6b">Opening
and Closing Windows</A> </LI>


<LI><A NAME="A54C0149e9"></A><A HREF="managewinds.html#A44C012b6d">Setting
Window Attributes and Constraints</A> </LI>


<LI><A NAME="C4EE421559lpas"></A><A HREF="managewinds.html#BC9D0F8612vbia">Controlling
Window Placement</A></LI>


<LI><A NAME="A54C0149ea"></A><A HREF="managewinds.html#A44C012b72">Changing
Windows Noninteractively</A></LI>


<LI><A NAME="A54C0149eb"></A><A HREF="managewinds.html#A8tk2130nita">Managing
Multiple Windows</A></LI>


<LI><A NAME="A54C0149ec"></A><A HREF="managewinds.html#A44C012b75">Other
Window Subroutines</A></LI></UL>


<P><A NAME="A3C0ED56617mhay"></A>GL provides subroutines to create and
manipulate windows from an application program. The windowing subroutines
are implemented on top of Enhanced X-Windows and work with any window
manager, including the AIXwindows window manager. A <I>GL
window</I> is one in which a GL application draws an image, while a <I>text
window</I> runs a shell. </P>


<H3><A NAME="A264X9395"></A>List of GL Window Subroutines<A NAME="INDEX772"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX773"></A> <A NAME="INDEX774"></A> <A NAME="INDEX775"></A>
<A NAME="INDEX776"></A> <A NAME="INDEX777"></A> </H3>


<TABLE><TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP" COLSPAN="2"><A NAME="A264X921b"></A><B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/blankscreen.html#A144X9128">blankscreen</A></B></TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</TD>


<TD>Turns screen refresh on and off.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP" COLSPAN="2"><A NAME="A264X921a"></A><B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/blanktime.html#A144X9178">blanktime</A></B></TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</TD>


<TD>Sets screen blanking timeout.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP" COLSPAN="2"><A NAME="A19C0e0d9"></A><B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/endfullscrn.html#laa350marj">endfullscrn</A></B></TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</TD>


<TD>Ends full screen mode.</TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP" COLSPAN="2"><A NAME="A318C9b95"></A><B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/fudge.html#A142X917a6">fudge</A></B></TD></TR>

<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</TD>

<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</TD>

<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD NOWRAP="NOWRAP" COLSPAN="2"><A NAME="A318C9ba9"></A><B><!--:libs:gl32tref:--><A HREF="../gl32tref/winposition.html#A142X9158d">winposition</A></B></TD></TR>


<TR VALIGN="TOP"><TD>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</TD>
```
